name: Uma Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm out the door at half five and at Brookend Farm by six. It's a dairy and barley place, about 180 cows, owned by the Marsh family, and I do the calves, the feeding and a lot of mucking out. I came to this late, three years ago, after twenty-eight years running a hospital kitchen. I'm still the slowest one there at most jobs, and the young lads tease me about it, but I love the mornings with the calves.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The calves, honestly. You get a sick one on the bottle and three days later it's butting your knees for more, and that's a good day. What wears me out is anything with a screen. The new feed wagon has a little computer in it and I just leave that to Danny. I've got a flip phone and I'm keeping it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, and I'd say it at the union meeting first. Every year somebody from a machinery firm says this box will change farming. Most of it ends up in a shed corner with a tarp over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I keep my job and my calves, and I'm glad. I'm not daft, I know the Marshes would buy a robot feeder tomorrow if it paid. If the clever stuff stays mostly talk, I get to finish out my working years the way I hoped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much changes. I'd keep doing my three mornings and two long days at Brookend, keep paying my union dues, and keep putting a bit by on top of my hospital pension. Maybe I'd finally let Danny show me the feed wagon screen, but I wouldn't promise that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. Like when the vet says it's only a bit of scour and nothing worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture the Marshes asking you to use some AI tool anyway, just for the farm records. What would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask who reads it and where it goes. When I was in the hospital kitchen they brought in a stock system that was meant to save us hours, and it just meant I typed everything twice. So I'd say fine, but somebody else does the typing, and I'd want the union to see what it collects about us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the Marshes would buy a robot feeder tomorrow if it paid. Does that sit in the back of your mind even now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. Mrs Marsh went to a demonstration day last spring and came back with a leaflet she left on the kitchen table, and I read it while I had my tea. It's just paper on a table until the price comes down. But I notice I don't throw those leaflets away, I put them back exactly where she left them.

S0.say: I'd tell the union meeting I told them so. Every year a machinery firm promises to change farming, and most of it ends up under a tarp in the corner of a shed.
S0.think: I keep my job and my calves, and I'm glad of it. I know the owners would buy a robot feeder tomorrow if it paid, so I'm relieved the clever stuff stays mostly talk.
S0.do: Keeps working her three mornings and two long days at Brookend Farm and keeps paying her union dues. Goes on putting a bit aside on top of her hospital pension, and might let a colleague show her the feed wagon screen.
S0.feel: Relieved, with a small worry about the owners' interest in robots that never quite leaves.
S0.quote: Every year somebody from a machinery firm says this box will change farming. Most of it ends up in a shed corner with a tarp over it.
S0.fieldNote: Uma is fiercely loyal to the work she chose late in life, and the calves are the heart of it. Even in the mildest picture she reaches for the union and asks who reads the data. Her past with a hospital stock system shapes her doubt about any screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need the union at the table before any of it comes in, not after. I'd say it on the farmworkers' group chat too, the one my daughter set up for me on the old tablet. The bosses get the savings and the workers get the leftovers, every single time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm the easiest one to drop. I'm 58, I'm still learning, and I can't work a screen. If the Marshes put in robot calf feeders, the calves were my whole job, and Danny can mind the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting and push for a proper agreement on new machines, with training paid for and nobody pushed out without notice. I'd talk to Jonas about whether I drop to three days and keep the calves. And I suppose I'd let Danny teach me the feed wagon, because it's better than being shown the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like weather coming in when the barley's not cut yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jonas the night the Marshes told you about a robot calf feeder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, that's that, and then I'd go and peel potatoes for an hour, because that's what I do when I'm cross. He'd say we don't need the money, and he'd be right, the house is paid off and I've got my pension. But it's not about the money. I came to farming to be out with animals, not to sit at home waiting to be sixty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said there are plenty of farm jobs nearby. Wouldn't you just move to another farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are plenty of farms round us, that's true, and they're always short of hands at calving. But if Brookend is putting in robots, the Hendersons up the road will do it two years later. I'd only be running from one shed to the next.

S1.say: I'd say the union needs to be at the table before any of it comes in, not after. The bosses get the savings and the workers get the leftovers every time.
S1.think: I'm the easiest one to drop at 58, still learning and no good with screens. If robot calf feeders arrive, my whole job goes and the younger man minds the machines.
S1.do: Goes to every union meeting and pushes for an agreement on new machines with paid training and notice. Talks to her partner about dropping to three days, and lets a colleague teach her the feed wagon controls.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like bad weather coming in before the harvest is in. Cross more than scared.
S1.quote: I came to farming to be out with animals, not to sit at home waiting to be sixty.
S1.fieldNote: Money isn't her worry; the house is paid off and she has a pension. What she fears is losing the purpose she found late in life. She blames owners and machine makers and would fight through the union before learning a screen, though she'd give in on the feed wagon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need laws, and fast. I'd be on the bus to the capital with the union banner, and I'd say it to anyone. You can't let a handful of companies switch off half the country's work in two years and call it progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be finished at Brookend by sixty, and I know it. A robot that can do the calves, the mucking out and the tractor, and never phones in sick? The Marshes would have to be saints not to buy it, and they're decent people, not saints.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I'd sit down with Jonas and our pension man and work out if I can stop at sixty without losing much, and I think I can. I'd march, I'd write to our member of parliament, and I'd push the union for a fund for older workers who get pushed out. In the first year after it arrives I'd probably be home, doing the allotment and helping my daughter with her little one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, really angry. And under the anger, sad, because I only just found this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one gives you two years of warning. What does that short a window change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is no time at all. With the calves you plan a year ahead at least, you breed in the spring for what you'll have next winter. I wouldn't even see one full round of my own work before it's gone. If they gave me ten years I'd be retired anyway and I'd just be fighting for the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Danny, and lads like him. He's 23, he's got a mortgage on a little terraced house and a baby due in March. I've got my pension and a paid-off roof. If anybody needs the union to win, it's him, not me.

S2.say: I'd say we need laws, and fast, and I'd be on the bus to the capital with the union banner. You can't let a few companies switch off half the country's work in two years and call it progress.
S2.think: I'd be finished at Brookend by sixty and I know it. The owners are decent people, but a robot that never phones in sick would be too good a deal to refuse.
S2.do: Sits down with her partner and pension adviser to plan stopping at sixty. Marches, writes to her member of parliament and pushes the union for a fund for older workers pushed out, then likely retires to her allotment and grandchild in the first year.
S2.feel: Really angry, and sad underneath, because she has only just found this work.
S2.quote: I wouldn't even see one full round of my own work before it's gone.
S2.fieldNote: She is financially safe and knows it, so her worry turns outward to younger colleagues with mortgages. The two-year window hurts because it cuts across the farming year she is still learning. Her response is political and collective, not personal retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, but I'd say we've got time to do it properly, so no excuses. Five years is enough to pass a law and set up proper retraining money. If the government sits on its hands for five years, that's a choice they've made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally it's not so bad. I'd be 63 in 2031, and I'd always pictured stopping somewhere around then. It takes away the choice of when, but it doesn't knock the ground out from under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Brookend for as long as they'd have me, and I'd get really stuck in with the union's campaign. I'd talk to the Marshes straight out and ask them what their plan is, because I'd rather know than guess. And I'd put the extra from my last few years' wages into the savings so Jonas and I can help the kids if their jobs go too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steadier. It's like knowing the date of an operation rather than being rushed in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned helping the kids. Whose job are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The kids. Leni's a nurse, so maybe she's safe longer, but Tomas drives a delivery van and they'll have robots doing that well before 2031. I'd want our savings ready to help him over a bad patch, even if it means no new kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said with two years you'd be retired by sixty, and here you'd keep going. Is the extra three years the whole difference for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I suppose I am. With two years I'd be swept out. With five I'd still not learn the screens, I'll be honest, but I'd have time to leave on my own feet with my head up, and to fight for the people coming after me.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough time to do it properly, so there are no excuses. If the government sits on its hands that long, that's a choice they've made.
S3.think: It's not so bad for me personally, because I'd be 63 and I always pictured stopping around then. It takes away the choice of when, not the ground under me.
S3.do: Keeps working at Brookend as long as she can and gets stuck in with the union's campaign. Asks the owners straight out about their plans, and saves her last years' wages to help her son if his delivery job goes.
S3.feel: Uneasy but steadier, like knowing the date of an operation rather than being rushed in.
S3.quote: I'd want our savings ready to help him over a bad patch, even if it means no new kitchen.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years matter to her mainly because they let her leave with dignity. She openly admits she still wouldn't learn the screens. Her worry shifts from herself to her son's delivery job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd better not waste it. I'd say it at the union branch and on the group chat. If we can't sort out decent rules and a decent safety net in ten years, we don't deserve the name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's honestly fine. I'd be 68 in 2036, and I'll be long done by then, God willing with my knees still working. It's the grandchildren I'd think about, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am at Brookend, calves and all, and stop when I'd planned to, around 63 or 64. I'd keep up the union work and maybe stand for the branch committee, because someone with time and no mortgage should do it. I wouldn't touch our savings plans at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit sad for the farm as it'll be, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandchildren about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them it'll be all right if people stick together, and I'd mean it. When the hospital kitchens went to frozen meals in the nineties. The ones who were in the union got moved or paid off properly, and the ones who weren't got nothing. That's the only lesson I've got and it's a good one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can you picture walking past Brookend in 2036 and seeing robots in the calf shed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. I'd be the old woman in the café saying I worked with calves by hand, you know. I'd like to think somebody would still keep a few animals the old way, even if just for the children to see.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd better not waste it. If we can't sort out decent rules and a safety net in ten years, we don't deserve the name.
S4.think: For me it's honestly fine, because I'd be 68 and long retired. It's my grandchildren I'd be thinking about, not myself.
S4.do: Carries on at Brookend as she is and retires around 63 or 64 as planned. Keeps up her union work and may stand for the branch committee, leaving her savings plans untouched.
S4.feel: Calm, with a little sadness for what the farm will become.
S4.quote: The ones who were in the union got moved or paid off properly, and the ones who weren't got nothing.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years the threat simply passes her by, and she knows it. Her one lesson from her kitchen years, that union members came through better, runs through every picture. She would use her free time to help others rather than to adapt herself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, the two years, no question. Not for me so much, I'll be all right, but for Danny and my son and everyone with a mortgage and little ones. What would help is a law that says if a robot takes your job, the firm pays into a fund that keeps you going and pays for real training, and the union gets a say in it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask why I came to farming at 55, and I'd tell you. After twenty-eight years cooking for sick people under strip lights, I wanted to see the sky. Don't let them take that away from people, that's all.

headlineQuote: After twenty-eight years cooking for sick people under strip lights, I wanted to see the sky.
portrait: Uma Schmidt is 58 and came to farming three years ago after running a hospital kitchen for 28 years. She looks after the calves at Brookend Farm, a dairy and barley farm, keeps a flip phone and leaves the feed wagon's computer to a younger colleague. Her house is paid off and she has a pension, so money never drives her worry; losing the outdoor work she found late in life does. She answers every picture through the union, blaming owners and machine makers, and she is most shaken by the two-year AGI picture, mainly for younger workers like her colleague Danny and her son, who drives a delivery van. With ten years she expects to be retired and calm.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture worries her most, less for herself than for younger workers with mortgages and her son who drives a delivery van.
whatWouldHelp: A law making firms that replace workers with robots pay into a fund that supports people and pays for real training, with the union having a say.
